title: Deciphering the Intricate Shell Microstructures of the 2700-Meter Deep-Sea Mussel Bathymodiolus marisindicus
content: Deciphering the shell microstructure enhances our understanding of the biological adaptation of deep-sea molluscs to their harsh living environments. The molluscs shells, as composite biomineralized material, have the role of providing mechanical strength and maintaining ecosystem services [1], in which, inorganic crystalline materials and organic layers are combined in complex forms, based on different hierarchical levels, and finally construct biomaterials [2]. Well-structured calcareous prismatic and nacreous layers in mussel shells have good mechanical properties and act as protective supports. For instance, freshwater mussel shells have been used as a replacement composition for fine and coarse aggregate in concrete, and different substitution rates were tested to yield the optimal compressive strength properties [3]. Due to the varying depths of their habitats, deep-sea mussel shells are anticipated to exhibit differences in layered microstructures compared to common freshwater mussel shells. Thus far, research on mussel shells has predominantly focused on freshwater species, as sample collection and pretreatments in deep-sea environments are technologically challenging, compounded by the ultra-high pressure and absence of light. Consequently, information regarding the shell microstructures of highly-structured, biomineralized deep-sea molluscs remains scarce.
